# Wrap-Up

<Twemoji tag="span">☕☕</Twemoji> Hello Little Rizzlers! We hope that you had a fun time solving puzzles and meeting friends at the Reunion!

Some quick statistics:

* 49 puzzles, including 6 metapuzzles and 1 capstone puzzle
* 2,420 individual participants among the 730 teams that solved at least one puzzle
* 251 teams finished at least one meta
* 140 teams finished the capstone
* 3,552 hints answered
* 14,398 total puzzles solved
* 43,943 total guesses made
* 42 sprites, 8 backgrounds, 12 custom graphics, 7 original compositions
* 15,500+ words over cutscenes and solve dialogue
* 6,900+ commits, 30,000+ lines of code

Heavy spoilers below!

## Plot summary

The hunt centered around a reunion of four friends who went to college together but have since drifted apart, Camille, Lam, Taylor, and Dawn (who goes by DJ at the beginning of the story). A few years after graduation, all four find themselves back in Riddleton for various reasons: Camille is visiting town for the weekend, Dawn moved in with her parents, Lam is attending a cardiology conference, and Taylor has been running a café called The Little Riddle.

Teams solved puzzles to unlock cutscenes involving the characters, watching them reconnect over the course of a few days in Riddleton. Each metapuzzle is based on the interpersonal relationship between two of the four characters, using answers from both characters’ rounds. After all six metapuzzles are solved, the four friends gather together at The Little Riddle to recap their reunion and reveal one final lesson, **LIFE IS BEST SOLVED TOGETHER**!

## Writing the hunt

### Goals and theme proposals

After Mystery Hunt 2026, we had a team-wide community survey about <Twemoji tag="span">✈✈✈</Twemoji> Galactic Trendsetters <Twemoji tag="span">✈✈✈</Twemoji> and Galactic Puzzle Hunt. There was less stated interest in running GPH 2026 than in previous years, including fewer people willing to take on leadership roles or produce art. We had enough momentum to start the writing process, but anticipated making a smaller GPH. This didn’t happen: compared to last year, we ended up writing more puzzles and producing more art.

Other than that, this year’s overall goals were similar to our usual ones: write good puzzles, hang out and have fun, involve more writers, and don’t burn ourselves out. The 11 initial theme proposals contained a mix of “wild” and “typical” ideas for the hunt structure. Three finalists were selected, and the winning proposal was titled “Romance\* Hunt”. (The asterisk led to a footnote saying “Romance not guaranteed.”)

### Theme and story

The winning theme involved four friends, each with their own round, and paired metas inspired by [Mystery Hunt 2019’s Holiday Forest](https://puzzles.mit.edu/2019/); this structure survived basically intact in the final hunt. The hunt was meant to be “four rounds and an endgame”, so individual puzzle writers had a lot of freedom, little tech work would be necessary, and time could be invested in story and art.

The vision of the theme was to write a story that was character-driven and relationship-focused, rather than having an overarching plot or problem. The setting and mood was only decided after several story meetings: other possibilities included a Psychonauts-inspired dreamscape, a Danganronpa-inspired high school murder mystery, a Zero Escape–inspired escape room, a story about superpowers, or a heist. In the end, we settled on a story that was much more grounded in reality: a reunion of college friends five years after graduation in Riddleton (“not-Cleveland”). It was a story about four mostly normal people, facing issues not unlike the ones we all face every day.

The idea was that the story should be focused on the four friends, avoiding supernatural elements or puzzle in-jokes that might “cheapen” the experience. For similar reasons, we chose to make the solvers and puzzles extrinsic elements from the story universe, since a solver-character would only intrude on the characters’ relationships.

Writing a story that was longer, more complex, and more serious than other GPH stories (and most other puzzlehunt stories in general) would be unexplored territory for us. Not to mention, it also had to include puzzles. The metapuzzles were written first, and the characters and story were written around them to match. We didn’t plan a global “plot”, or inasmuch as there was one, we allowed it to blossom organically from the individual arcs.

The original theme proposal loosely imagined that solvers would be able to ship any two of the four characters, for a total of six possible romances. However, this changed substantially after all metapuzzles had been proposed, leaving only one storyline with anything resembling romance (Lam+Taylor). The other five pairs developed their relationships in completely different ways, perhaps vaguely leaving the door open to “the possibility of romance” farther in the future.

### Puzzle structure and endgame

As discussed above, the structure of four “character rounds” and six paired metapuzzles was determined early on by the theme proposal. We wanted metas to take “6 or 7” answers to end up at a 40-puzzle hunt, but we found it challenging to come up with pairing mechanics using 6 or fewer answers. We ended up with three 6-puzzle metas and three 8-puzzle metas, for a total of 42 puzzles, which was more puzzles than we were aiming for.

Metas were primarily tested individually, with both sides padded with made-up answers to simulate the difficulty of matching puzzles to their metas (“metamatching”). Much later, we ran a metamatching testsolve where testers were given every answer in the hunt, which confirmed that:

* Personality Conflict was the easiest
* Birth Charts was not necessarily the easiest meta, but had easy metamatching
* The food items in Menu Update were distinctive
* The colorful answers in Figuration were distinctive

As many solvers experienced, the hardest part of the metamatching was teasing apart the answers for Amorous Appointments, Heart-to-Heart, and the non-Dawn side of Figuration. Later, we reassigned two character pairs for plot reasons (Figuration used to be the Dawn+Taylor meta, and Heart-to-Heart used to be Dawn+Lam), which technically invalidated the metamatching testsolve (“it's fiiiiiiiiiine” <Twemoji tag="span">🤞</Twemoji>). Fortunately, we don’t think this significantly affected the metamatching difficulty in the actual hunt.

For puzzle unlocking, we chose to unlock the puzzles in a single global order, making sure that the puzzles for different characters unlocked evenly and that the harder puzzles were spread across the entire hunt (except for the beginning and the end). Every solve unlocked at least one new puzzle (although if a cutscene unlocked along with it, it was necessary to watch that first), but we also made harder puzzles contribute to expanding width: solving one of the longest/hardest puzzles (Grid Adventure, Fuzzy Logic, Realism) would guarantee a second unlock, while solving other puzzles would increase width by a fractional amount based on our internal estimate of each puzzle’s difficulty/length. The overall width increase from puzzles was a bit more generous than usual in case teams didn’t solve enough harder puzzles. This had the effect that teams who solved the hard puzzles had higher width than usual towards the end of the hunt. We also considered separate progression and unlocks inside each round, but the risk of teams getting bottlenecked in one round seemed too high (did Taylor have any easy puzzles?).

We discussed writing an intro round or small micropuzzle round, plausibly themed around "The Little Riddle", but we had little puzzle-writing power to spare, and the hunt felt big enough as it was. Instead, we added a few small pre-hunt dialogues to gently introduce our characters. In lieu of an explicit round of easy puzzles, we tried to put more approachable puzzles at the beginning and make them easier where applicable — although the first few puzzles were still harder on average than last year's intro round, based on your feedback.

The final endgame involved two stages, the first chronologically sorting all of the cutscenes, and the second extracting the final answer from an overlapping-letters mechanic. The chronological sort idea had been around since early brainstorming meetings, though as usual, endgame wasn’t written until a few days before the hunt. We were still rewriting scenes until a few minutes before hunt, tightening some clues for the chronological ordering as well as just checking for consistency.

### Writing timeline

* March 11: kickoff meeting
* March 30: Romance\* Hunt theme selected
* April: character archetypes fleshed out, cutscene interface brainstormed
* May 4: two metas written
* June 20: full metamatching testsolve
* July 13: wanted 15/42 puzzles in testsolving, but only had 10, so the hunt was delayed from September 11 to October 9. We initially delayed to September 25, then to October 9 because of a scheduling conflict with enigame.
* August 24: 13 puzzles in testsolving, ≥1 sprite per character and café background drawn
* September 11: cutscene UI redesign, initial recording of background music, art and story push
* September 26: full hunt testsolve by external solvers (excluding capstone). Begin factchecking and final story writing
* October 5: capstone written, ~75% of cutscene text written
* October 9: hunt start!

## Reflections

### Theme

We chose a story-centered theme partly as a nice change of pace from recent GPHs which have involved a lot of global puzzle design constraints. This wasn’t an absolute goal for the hunt; competing theme proposals had their fair share of wild ideas. But the winning theme promised a return to full creative flexibility for individual puzzles, combined with the idea of a cozy story. We think that there are advantages to both approaches, either trying an innovative global puzzle structure, or letting the puzzles be more normal and focusing on story, polish, or something else.

### Puzzle writing and balance

Puzzle-writing fell behind this year, even further behind than usual GPH (on 8/24, 1.5 months from the hunt, only 13 puzzles were at or beyond testsolving). We had fewer active authors than past years and a larger number of puzzles to write (so much so that we considered cutting one of the six metapuzzles, but this seemed like a huge compromise in hunt structure). In the last few weeks, a few “guest authors” contributed puzzles. So we whiffed on the goal of having a smaller hunt and getting people more involved <Twemoji tag="span">🙁</Twemoji>

We think the lack of puzzle-writing activity led to less room for editorial control and rejecting puzzle ideas, and also some puzzles the authors privately considered uninspired. Then again, we very rarely reject a puzzle idea in general (if a puzzle doesn’t get written, it’s usually because the author ran out of time or motivation). Most of this year’s puzzles were written by returning authors, who need less editorial assistance — so perhaps some amount of writing puzzles under duress can still produce decent results.

Galactic Puzzle Hunt skews its topics due to biases among the hunt writers; mainly, there were a lot of video games. Other recurring topics we noticed: puzzlehunt encodings, card games, cryptics, unlabeled graphs, and New York. Another unusual and unresolved issue was that we had a lot of puzzles with nondescript one-word plural noun titles: Alternates, Halves, Revisions, Scores, Sketches, Strays, Vowels, Wavelengths, Oops.

The hunt’s difficulty seemed slightly higher than recent years, in our opinion. This was partly offset by the use of free answers (which many solvers really liked).

### Plot–puzzle integration

Metapuzzles were mostly written with little more direction than to be vaguely themed around two-person relationships. As with puzzles, we didn’t have a lot of meta proposals, so there wasn’t a lot of room for picking the ones that were most thematic or best for plot. (The main exception was Menu Update, which was developed with the Little Riddle café firmly in mind.) This pushed most of the difficulty onto the story team, who did an impressive job spaghetti-ing the characters and their stories out of the metas. This isn’t the best way to write a story, but it felt more urgent to finish metapuzzles early so that puzzle-writing could start.

Every meta involved combining answers from one character with another, and in fact every meta involved pairing up every answer with one other answer. We didn’t originally plan for the latter property, but all the metas other than Figuration developed as an answer-pairing meta. This perhaps influenced the final Figuration implementation we chose from among several competing ideas. (The “trans” theme and the colors of the trans flag were involved in early drafts of Figuration, but in a completely different way; the colors were not in the answers themselves until basically the final version.)

Early on, we hoped to assign puzzles to characters in ways that were thematic to their personalities. For example, Lam would have logic puzzles, or Dawn would have interactive puzzles. This mostly didn’t work; we let authors develop the kinds of puzzles they wanted, instead of enforcing quotas like “We need 10 logic puzzles” or “We need 10 interactive puzzles”. To the extent it worked it was a coincidence.

Ways metas shaped our characters:

* **Camille:** The first character we brainstormed. We wanted characters that puzzle solvers might relate to and we liked the idea of having a trivia nerd. The first two metas we wrote were Personality Conflict and Birth Charts, which seemed to fit the trivia nerd well, probably being a little into pseudoscience and woo. Thus, Camille. (Eventually we thought “wow, this character has 2 metas about getting into arguments with people.” So we made Camille more outspoken.)

* **Taylor:** From early on, we wanted the characters to meet up at a café which one of the characters would run. Taylor was always fairly straightforward: he’s the guy you can talk to if you’re having a rough day, he’ll do his best to listen, and he’ll brew you some coffee if you’re feeling down (“It’s on the house!”). He basically did not change at all over the course of the hunt’s development (other than originally being a girl in the first draft). We originally had Figuration between Taylor and Dawn, but eventually decided that Heart-to-Heart worked better for the characters.

* **Lam:** The concept of a “southeast Asian immigrant doctor” character came up pretty early. We originally conceived of her as being pretty serious and logical (to conflict with Camille in Birth Charts), but making her a little snarky added a lot in the end. She ended up getting paired with Dawn for Figuration, so we also needed her to be someone you could easily open up to, as well as having some experience with being trans (despite being cis herself). That said, she was a guy in the first draft. I guess we transed everyone except Camille. Also, her name was originally Lau, until Amorous Appointments testsolvers connected Taylor and Lau to Taylor Lautner and got rabbit-holed by an interesting bit of celebrity trivia — he [married a different Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Lautner#Personal_life), resulting in both of them being named Taylor Lautner.

* **DJ/Dawn:** We wanted to write a meta where solving the meta helps one of the characters realize they’re trans (Figuration). The meta pun was brilliant, and so this became Dawn. We needed a different name pre-meta, so we chose “DJ” as a less-gendered D-name. Dawn was probably the last of the characters we fully defined; outside of the nebulous categories of “trans” and “gamer”, we didn’t really have much to go off here. After several metas were assigned, we arbitrarily assigned Dawn to the remaining ones (Personality Conflict and Heart-to-Heart), and tried to write her from there. Personality Conflict was particularly difficult, since we had originally conceived of Camille and Dawn getting along really well. Dawn being an artist was inspired by the Heart-to-Heart answer pun.

### Writing a candid story

In most hunts, the story is something of an afterthought; for ours, we really wanted the story to be central, and to inspire solvers to care about it. This was pretty ambitious for us and we knew it wasn’t going to be easy, especially since none of us had actually written anything comparable, much less as a collective effort. We did have an inkling of what needed to be done, though. And as with previous hunts, we were crazy enough to try anyway.

We had decided that the story moments would be deeply themed around the metapuzzles, reflecting not just their answers and theming, but ideally also their solve process. This posed a number of constraints on the characters and interactions, which turned out to be the biggest challenge in the writing process. In particular, we wanted the six different interactions to be emotionally moving, yet integrated into four coherent characters and a cohesive timeline, all while keeping the interactions sufficiently distinct so as not to spoil one story from within another.

Early on (April–June), a lot of work went into fleshing out the characters and figuring out how they all fit together, along with some initial drafting work. But we fell into a bit of a story-writing rut up until two weeks before the hunt, largely because we were mostly focused on puzzle-writing up to that point. At that point, there were still many unresolved questions, most scenes still felt mechanical, and many meta scenes were not written altogether.

<Image
  nameWithExt="wrapup/alignment-chart.png"
  caption="Jokingly-created personality alignment chart for the main characters."
/>

With renewed focus and more hands in the last two weeks, things started to fall into place. Based on the initial drafting work, we decided on having exactly four cutscenes for each character pair, and redrafted a provisional timeline. The four-part structure would loosely serve as introduction, development, climax and resolution for each of the metapuzzle themes, but we favored organically intermixing themes in the first two parts for each pair over sticking to any one formula.

Most of the initial drafts, and even many aspects of the initial characters and interactions, did not survive the final two-week push – and that was part of the process. Through a stressful process of drafting, reviewing and redrafting, mostly concentrated in the last week, right up to the night before, we wrangled out a consistent timeline, consistent character motivations, and coherent emotional states, all while maintaining the story’s emotional core and keeping the characters relatable. Beyond that, the final metapuzzle and most of the art was produced within that two week timeframe, as they were mostly contingent on story.

Looking to make a serious puzzle hunt story of your own? Here are some tips from the writers’ table:

* **Draft early, shamelessly, repeatedly.** At the beginning, it’s gonna feel like you have no good ideas. Characters feel stereotypical and one-dimensional. Draft their interactions anyway. The first drafts will suck, as ours did, but they concretize the characters, leading you to ask more questions and explore them more deeply – and that’s where the emotional weight and complexity come from.

  Every draft feels awkward, stupid, and a waste of time just before you write it. And once a draft is written, it’s natural to feel like it’s “work done” and feel unwilling to discard it or change it significantly, _especially_ if it’s written by someone else.

  Don’t do this. We were only able to get the depth of writing we wanted by redrafting over existing drafts, and heavily modifying or discarding entire drafts and plot ideas when it worked better for the story. When something doesn’t seem right and you’re not sure if a redraft would make it better, draft a fork instead of directly overwriting the text, then review with co-writers what ultimately feels better. And have a clear agreement among writers from the outset that everyone is comfortable with anything they write potentially not getting used.

* **Aim to tell a story, not satisfy requirements.** A lot of friction in our writing process arose from trying to fit meta constraints that were more artificial than we realized, or trying to conform to ideas set out by the initial drafts, or the initial draft timeline we proposed for how scenes would fit together. Having a rough plan of the plot and requirements initially can be helpful as a guide, but translating that into a list of scenes with a long list of requirements for each of them leads to mechanical prose and characters behaving in unnatural ways that eats at the plot’s emotional core.

  Instead, focus on the characters’ motivations and emotional state, and think about how they would actually react to the interactions and scenarios you present them with. Sometimes, you’ll find that a character must bring something up or act a certain way in response to a scenario. Those are your real requirements. If they conflict with the requirements you had for the scene, then those requirements need to be revisited, the characters reviewed, the timeline redrafted. Major changes may be required, but that’s where the most interesting parts of the story come from – weaving the characters through time and having _them_ lead the plot, not the other way round.

* **Make characters feel different in more than just superficial ways.** Characters are essential to writing, perhaps more so for emotional stories than any other kind of writing. On the surface, it may seem crazy that most of our entire story was written in two weeks, at least in terms of what text actually got used. But the reality is (apart from the hours of sleep lost in those two weeks) that most of the groundwork was laid out before when the characters were designed and explored in the initial drafts.

  One of the main goals we had in the early stages was to make the characters _feel_ as different as possible. This goes beyond superficial details like occupation, hobbies and quirks – we wanted each character to have an entire _vibe_. They view the world in different ways, differing not just in personality and background, but in their deepest motivations and insecurities. This affects everything, from how they act, to how they talk, to how they look. While the superficial themes of their interactions were ultimately constrained by the metas, the cores of their interactions ultimately sprout naturally from how they as characters conflict and complement each other. Things like hobbies and background should be treated as fluid in the writing process – be willing to revisit them if they lead to awkward interactions, or if changing them would lead to a more interesting story.

* **Have multiple writers.** This is the most important. One person with reviewers can produce a reasonable story, but multiple writers make a much better story much faster. Writers need to contribute not just ideas in brainstorming, but actual, concrete drafts – which in our case, meant interaction dialogue. When it comes to an emotional story at least, most of the juice comes out naturally through actually playing out the interactions between characters, and this is colored strongly by the perspectives and experiences of the writer.

  Even though most of the writing in the last two weeks was done by only a few writers, “a few” instead of “one” was what made all the difference. The effect is non-linear – a single writer, especially not an experienced one, simply does not have enough lived experience to write multiple interesting, distinct characters. In fact, the months-long rut we experienced before that can mostly be attributed to the lack of availability of more than one writer, or one writer’s drafts being treated as final product.

  After all, as they say – (writing slice of) life is best solved together.

While investing huge amounts of effort into the story, we also had to ask ourselves, how do we encourage solvers to engage with it? After all, GPH is still a puzzlehunt, primarily distinguished from other media by having puzzles. We wanted the story to be engaging enough that people would “come for the puzzles, stay for the story,” and many teams wrote in our feedback form that this worked! Mechanically, we tried to give every opportunity to engage with the story, for example by making the cutscenes thematically relevant to the metas (most apparent for Figuration). To encourage taking one’s time with the hunt, we also grouped the scoreboard and set updates to once per hour, an approach inspired by [Teammate Hunt 2025](https://2025.teammatehunt.com/).

### LLM usage

(We realize that opinions on LLMs are divisive. Below are some reflections on our experience running GPH 2026 and ideas for how future puzzle hunts might adapt.)

This is the second year with our rule against using an LLM to solve a puzzle or a significant part of one. Since last year, LLMs have drastically improved at solving puzzles. We ran some informal checks ourselves ahead of time and were reasonably confident that a frontier LLM could solve most of this year’s puzzles and likely finish the hunt, though with some amusing lapses (for example, on Normal Quiz, the LLM answered all questions on its first try except for recognizing the artist from the audio clip). So we knew that any team that turned to an LLM would be able to get an advantage, especially on heavy-computation/work puzzles such as Fuzzy Logic, Multi-Hyphenates, and Arithmetic Circuit.

We’re not aware of any LLMs doing the hunt autonomously, but we know at least some teams plugged some puzzles into LLMs. In the interest of fairness and according to our rules, we hid known cases from the team scoreboard. In many of the cases we detected, teams were solving certain puzzles much faster than humanly possible; asking an LLM to solve a puzzle you just unlocked is totally against the spirit of the puzzle hunt. On the other hand, we recognize that norms around LLM usage vary among teams and communities, e.g. a team might paste a puzzle into an LLM to overcome a language/accessibility barrier or to bypass grunt work. In some cases, teams may have unintentionally violated our rules, thinking that their LLM usage was within the allowed scope. We apologize to teams that felt unfairly treated by this policy — this is a developing technology, and we hope that expectations will be clearer in the future as the boundaries set by the puzzle hunt community become more defined. Since there were probably other cases that were not detected or did not have sufficient evidence to act on, please take this year’s scoreboard with a grain of salt.

We doubt that any online hunt can make LLM use impossible or not advantageous, which means it’s going to be tricky to maintain the competitive aspects of online hunts. It seems like a good time to experiment with ideas that discourage or disincentivize LLM usage more strongly: perhaps 2027 should be the year of in-person or paper-based puzzle hunts, or the global leaderboard could be replaced by [Advent of Code](https://adventofcode.com/)-style private leaderboards which allow smaller communities to set their own rules.

Should we allow teams to use LLMs to improve their own puzzle solving experience by skipping parts of puzzles that are too hard for them? We think that good puzzle hunt design should try to eliminate the desire for this usage. This may require rethinking how teams progress through the hunt, since the current paradigm locks interesting content behind solving hard puzzles. As of now, we encourage teams who want to use LLMs to treat them as a narrow-use tool (like how Google can get you unstuck on a newspaper crossword puzzle, but it’s no longer a “clean” solve). After all, being stuck on a puzzle, and then figuring it out, is part of what makes puzzle solving fun! For our part, we will continue to write puzzle hunts designed for humans to solve without the help of an LLM.

We had no official policy on LLM use for constructing the hunt. Some authors used LLMs for puzzle construction or solution writing assistance, and the web team used significant LLM assistance to build the website, especially implementing the interactive puzzle interfaces. On the other hand, every puzzle idea was proposed and edited by humans. LLMs were not used for producing any art, dialogue, music, or responses to hint requests.

### Web

Every year we think “the tech team can rest”, and every year this doesn’t happen because work expands xP. Partly this was because LLM coding assistants have become much more powerful since last year (we tried using an LLM to write the jigsaw piece/puzzle logic in 2025, but the results were extremely dissatisfying). This raised our ambitions for the hunt website’s interface:

* We implemented a complex VN cutscene UI with a variety of features, including a separate log view, per-character and full-page animations, cued sound effects, and keyboard and scroll wheel inputs. Separately, we had the characters show up in puzzles for post-solve dialogue (particularly Wordtris’s dialogue, which was dynamic, and Two Years Later’s dialogue, which features an interesting cameo).

* We added bespoke synced interfaces to allow solvers to collaboratively solve Wordtris, Grid Adventure, and Goodbye directly on our website.

* We included a lot of tooltips, diagrams, and other details to solutions, e.g. the wordplay annotations and encodings in the [Cryptic Codewords solution](https://2026.galacticpuzzlehunt.com/solution/cryptic-codewords), or the visualizer in the [Realism solution](https://2026.galacticpuzzlehunt.com/solution/realism).

* We gave ourselves ever more features for administering the hunt, like allowing hint-givers to see teams’ progress on the aforementioned interactive puzzles directly on the hint page.

* We supported a [puzzle](https://2026.galacticpuzzlehunt.com/puzzle/arrows) <Arrows seq=". ese nn sw wnw nnw * ss nw w nne n ee ssw ssw wsw sse" /> whose title was not even a Unicode string.

* We changed <DJ />’s name to Dawn dynamically.

We hope that you enjoyed these new features! Fortunately for everyone, the server did not experience any major issues or outages during the hunt.

### Other new things we tried

* **Post-solve dialogue.** After each puzzle was solved, the characters would have a little post-solve banter. People loved it. The idea here was to ensure that even if people weren’t watching the cutscenes, they still got to see the characters interact with each other. Plus, it gave writers a little opportunity to comment on the puzzle content itself, which you don’t normally see in hunts.

* **Free answers.** People loved them. We gave each team 4 throughout the hunt, which seemed about right.

* **Insights.** We piloted “insights” for certain puzzles, which were hints in the form of mini-examples of an aha or mechanic for the puzzle, an idea inspired by [Can of Wormholes](https://store.steampowered.com/app/1295320/Can_of_Wormholes/). We found them hard to write and weren’t sure how useful they would be, but people generally liked them, so we consider the pilot a success.

* **Scoreboard.** The scoreboard was organized in groups and only updated once per hour. We heard mixed opinions about this: some people admitted that a less addictive feed was better for their health, while others felt the scoreboard became kind of useless. We think a best-of-both-worlds version might be possible. Also see our discussion about overall competitiveness in the “LLM usage” section.

* **Hints.** In previous years, hints could have unlimited follow-ups, whereas this year they were limited to at most one follow-up. We changed this mostly to prevent really long back-and-forth hint conversations that go nowhere, and found it to be a huge improvement in that regard. We also cut the option for hints of different “sizes”, based on last year’s feedback.

* **Post-hunt checkers.** We added various work checkers after the hunt ended (for example, see [Make Your Own Cheryl’s Birthday](https://2026.galacticpuzzlehunt.com/hints/make-your-own-cheryls-birthday) or [Genetic Code](https://2026.galacticpuzzlehunt.com/hints/genetic-code)). This might’ve been good during-hunt for hint-givers checking solvers’ work, or perhaps to help solvers somehow.

Did we actually get “less hints than usual” because of free answers and insights?

* Last year: average 3.61 hints per active team out of 15 total hint tokens. This year: average 2.99 out of 13. About 5% usage of all possible hints for both years.

* Free answers didn’t seem to impact hint usage, based on number of hints per day or compared to 2025.

* Insights reduced hints for some puzzles (but the error bars for these estimated reductions are huge):

  * 6 7 and Soup of the Day were reduced by 75%, Stacked reduced by 50%
  * World Connections reduced by 33%, Strays by 30%, Cryptic Codewords by 50%
